shared_context.topic: How to tell a canker sore from herpes

atoms.1: To differentiate between a canker sore and a herpes lesion, consider the following characteristics:
atoms.2: Location: Canker sores (aphthous ulcers) typically occur inside the mouth on the soft tissues, such as the inner cheeks, lips, tongue, or the base of the gums.
atoms.3: Location: Herpes lesions (caused by herpes simplex virus) often appear on the lips (cold sores) or around the mouth.
atoms.4: Herpes lesions can also occur inside the mouth, particularly on the hard palate or gums.
atoms.5: Appearance: Canker sores are usually small, round or oval, with a white or yellow center and a red border.
atoms.6: Appearance: Herpes lesions start as small, fluid-filled blisters that eventually burst and form painful ulcers.
atoms.7: Pain and Sensation: Canker sores are typically painful, especially when eating or talking.
atoms.8: Pain and Sensation: Canker sores do not cause systemic symptoms.
atoms.9: Pain and Sensation: Herpes lesions can be painful and may be preceded by a tingling or burning sensation.
atoms.10: Pain and Sensation: Herpes lesions can be associated with systemic symptoms such as fever, swollen lymph nodes, and malaise.
atoms.11: Recurrence and Triggers: Canker sores are not caused by a virus and are not contagious.
atoms.12: Recurrence and Triggers: Canker sores can be triggered by factors such as stress, minor mouth injuries, acidic or spicy foods, and certain medical conditions.
atoms.13: Recurrence and Triggers: Herpes lesions are caused by the herpes simplex virus.
atoms.14: Recurrence and Triggers: The herpes simplex virus remains dormant in the body and can reactivate, leading to recurrent outbreaks.
atoms.15: Recurrence and Triggers: Triggers for herpes lesions include stress, illness, sunlight, and hormonal changes.
atoms.16: Diagnosis: Canker sores are usually diagnosed based on clinical appearance and history.
atoms.17: Diagnosis: No specific tests are typically required for diagnosing canker sores.
atoms.18: Diagnosis: Herpes lesions can be diagnosed through clinical examination.
atoms.19: Diagnosis: Confirmation of herpes lesions may require laboratory tests such as viral culture, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), or serologic tests for herpes simplex virus antibodies.

snippets.output: To differentiate between a canker sore and a herpes lesion, consider the following characteristics: location, appearance, pain and sensation, recurrence and triggers, and diagnosis.

Location: Canker sores typically occur inside the mouth on the soft tissues, such as the inner cheeks, lips, tongue, or the base of the gums. Herpes lesions often appear on the lips or around the mouth and can also occur inside the mouth, particularly on the hard palate or gums.

Appearance: Canker sores are usually small, round or oval, with a white or yellow center and a red border. Herpes lesions start as small, fluid-filled blisters that eventually burst and form painful ulcers.

Diagnosis: Canker sores are usually diagnosed based on clinical appearance and history, with no specific tests typically required. Herpes lesions can be diagnosed through clinical examination, but confirmation may require laboratory tests such as viral culture, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), or serologic tests for herpes simplex virus antibodies.

Canker sores (aphthous ulcers) are typically painful, especially when eating or talking, whereas herpes lesions (herpes simplex/cold sores) can also be painful and may be preceded by a tingling or burning sensation.

Canker sores (aphthous ulcers) do not cause systemic symptoms, whereas herpes lesions (herpes simplex/cold sores) can be associated with systemic symptoms such as fever, swollen lymph nodes, and malaise.

Canker sores (aphthous ulcers) are not caused by a virus, are not contagious, and can be triggered by stress, minor mouth injuries, acidic or spicy foods, and certain medical conditions, whereas herpes lesions (herpes simplex/cold sores) are caused by the herpes simplex virus.

Herpes lesions (herpes simplex/cold sores) can recur because the herpes simplex virus remains dormant in the body and can reactivate, and triggers for herpes lesions include stress, illness, sunlight, and hormonal changes.
